rationale: B wins because it treats uncertainty as material, not decorative. Its "220 million users, 24,000 paying teams: Canva's enterprise push is a conversion problem in numbers" turns the supplied numbers into a clean reporter question, while A's "Notion, Figma, and Miro ran the same arc" imports a template the update did not earn. A has usable bones, but B is the set I would let near a founder before a live pitch.
gaps_in_A: "Notion, Figma, and Miro ran the same arc. Canva is the largest consumer-originated design tool to attempt it." Outside facts and an unsupported superlative. That is how a smart angle gets lazy.
"already inside companies" stretches 220M monthly users into enterprise penetration without evidence; A later admits the 24,000 paid teams may be tiny startups.
"so the legal team can make a slide deck without asking design" invents a user, workflow, and internal tension. Good color, bad fact discipline.
"Enterprise contracts introduce stickier, higher-ASP revenue and reduce churn risk" states the finance thesis as fact despite no pricing, contract size, churn, or revenue mix.
gaps_in_B: "moving its sales motion into accounts the incumbents already own" still assumes account-level overlap the update does not prove.
"Canva takes aim at Adobe and Microsoft" is accurate but obvious. The body sharpens it; the headline is still launch-news wallpaper.
"The protagonist is the user base" makes the data angle tidy but abstract; it needs historical conversion data or a real buyer before it becomes more than arithmetic.
"run newsjack-detector on Adobe and Microsoft" is useful, but only if it finds a real live peg. Do not bolt on a fake competitive hook just because the workflow can search for one.
